title: Psalm 3:1–8
context: Psalm 3 is David’s cry when he fled from Absalom: foes multiply, and many say there is no salvation for him in God—yet the LORD is a shield about him, his glory, and the lifter of his head. He cries and is answered from the holy hill; he lies down, sleeps, and wakes sustained; he will not fear thousands arrayed against him. He pleads for the LORD to arise and save, for God strikes enemies and breaks the wicked’s teeth—and confesses that salvation belongs to the LORD, whose blessing rests on his people.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on multiplying foes, the taunt that God will not save, the shield and lifter of the head, sleep under the LORD’s sustaining hand, and salvation belonging to God alone—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Psalm 3:1–8.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English editions of the sources named.

arminian.quote: David complains to God of his enemies, comforts himself in God and the experience of his goodness, and triumphs in the salvation of God. My soul—of me: the soul being commonly put for the person. In God—God hath utterly forsaken him. Selah—probably a musical note, directing the singer either to lift up his voice, to make a pause, or to lengthen the tune; generally placed at some remarkable passage, to quicken the attention of singer and hearer. A shield—my defence. My glory—thou hast formerly given, and wilt farther give occasion of glorying in thy power and favour. Lifter up—thou wilt restore me to my former power and dignity. His hill—out of heaven. Slept—securely, casting all my cares upon God. Awaked—after a sweet and undisturbed sleep. Cheek bone—which implies contempt and reproach. Teeth—their strength and the instruments of their cruelty; he compares them to wild beasts. Salvation belongeth unto the LORD: thy blessing is upon thy people.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Psalm 3)

reformed.quote: David, although driven from his kingdom and pressed with despair of relief from every earthly quarter, ceases not to call upon God, and supports himself from his promise against the greatest terrors, the mockery of enemies, and death itself. After he had humbled himself before God and obtained forgiveness, he was persuaded God was on his side and would protect his kingdom; yet he complained of the conspiracy because they wickedly rose to frustrate God’s decree. Many say to his soul there is no help for him in God—their boldness grew because they thought him a castaway; the godly must give ear to God alone and cherish the hope of the salvation he has promised. Jehovah is a shield, his glory, and the lifter of his head: defended by God’s power, he walks with unabashed brow. He cried with his voice and was heard from the holy hill—prayer proving faith amid distress. He slept and awoke because the LORD sustained him—faith allaying anxiety so he reposed in God. Salvation belongeth unto the Lord: deliverance is only in God’s hands; though a thousand deaths hang over his people, God can save them, and this care is for the whole Church, whose welfare hung on David’s kingdom.
reformed.source: Commentary on the Book of Psalms (on Psalm 3)

verses.text: O LORD, how many are my foes! Many are rising against me;
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley opens the psalm as David’s complaint of enemies who have increased and risen against him—Absalom’s revolt in view.

Arminian hearing: the cry is honest prayer, not theatrical despair. Multiplied foes are real; the next verses will answer with trust. Shared piety—bring the count of enemies to the LORD rather than nurse them alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: David was nearly as many enemies as subjects; sudden rebellion affrighted him. It was uncommon faith, when so smitten, to pour out his soul to God. The only remedy for fear is to cast cares upon him.

Reformed accent: shared—complaint that still prays. Consternation does not cancel address to God; those who think themselves disregarded are the ones overwhelmed.

verses.text: many are saying of my soul, “There is no salvation for him in God.” Selah
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: My soul—of me; the soul put for the person. In God—God hath utterly forsaken him. Selah marks a remarkable passage and quickens attention.

Arminian pastoral: the taunt is blasphemous counsel—deny hope in God and the soul is pierced. Shared confession—the lie must not be believed. Keep praying for salvation when many say there is none.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: enemies deride him as a castaway past hope; their boldness grew because they thought God had rejected him. Absalom hoped from his own power, disregarding God. Though the whole world drive us to despair, give ear to God alone and cherish the hope of the salvation he has promised.

Reformed accent: shared—the mockery wounds the soul. Ungodliness treats God’s favor as worthless; faith answers by defending the soul in prayer.

verses.text: But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: A shield—my defence. My glory—thou hast formerly given, and wilt farther give occasion of glorying in thy power and favour. Lifter up—thou wilt restore me to my former power and dignity.

Arminian reading: against the taunt of v. 2 stands a living “but you.” Shield, glory, and lifted head name grace received and still to be sought—defence now, restoration expected. Trust answers the many who deny salvation in God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: but—confidence against scoffings. Having mourned sin and obtained mercy, David keeps his eye on the cause: enemies wage ungodly war against a lawful king. God is shield (defence by his power), glory (maintainer of the royal dignity he conferred), and lifter of the head—so he walks with unabashed brow.

Reformed accent: shared—the LORD himself is shield and glory. Assurance rests on God’s choice and promise that foes cannot cancel, not on counting friends in the wilderness.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess that the LORD—not the crowd—is shield, glory, and lifter of the head against the taunt that God will not save. Arminian readers, with Wesley, stress defence already given and restoration still sought: glorying in favour that will lift the head again. Reformed readers, with Calvin, stress that after repentance David rests on God’s unchanged appointment of the king—power that defends the dignity God conferred against a conspiracy meant to frustrate his decree.

verses.text: I cried aloud to the LORD, and he answered me from his holy hill. Selah
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: His hill—out of heaven, so called (Ps 15:1).

Arminian pastoral: shared pattern—cry aloud, and God answers. Voice prayer meets the tumult of foes. The answer from the holy hill confirms that the shield of v. 3 is not theory; keep crying when enemies say there is no salvation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: never so broken as to stop praying—an infallible proof of faith. He cried with his voice against blasphemies that would silence him, and was heard from the holy hill—Mount Zion and the ark, not a vague sky. Even far from the ark in flight, God was near to hear.

Reformed accent: shared—answered prayer. Faith speaks aloud toward the place God appointed; the answer proves the cry was not empty air.

verses.text: I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Slept—securely, casting all my cares upon God. Awaked—after a sweet and undisturbed sleep.

Arminian hearing: sleep here is practiced trust—cares cast, then rest. Shared comfort—the LORD sustains through the night. Fear does not get the last word when the sleeper entrusts himself and rises again.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: wonderful steadfastness—he slept amid many deaths as if beyond danger. Anxiety’s waves were allayed by faith so he reposed in God. This rest came from God’s protection, not stupidity; the wicked sleep by intoxication, but David because upheld by God’s power.

Reformed accent: shared—sleep and waking under the LORD. The ground of quiet is that God sustains; the godly prove victorious over fears because they rely on him.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess real sleep and waking because the LORD sustains the threatened servant. Arminian readers, with Wesley, stress casting cares upon God—secure sleep as practiced trust that still must entrust. Reformed readers, with Calvin, stress that faith’s quiet is wrought because God upholds: repose rests on divine protection, not on a covenant with death or numb indifference.

verses.text: I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s notes leave the verse to stand with the sustaining of v. 5: fear yields when God has kept through the night.

Arminian pastoral: shared courage—“I will not be afraid” is a resolve fed by prior help. Thousands may encircle; the sustained sleeper answers with refusal of panic. Courage is grace-enabled and still chosen against the ring of foes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he enlarges the efficacy of confidence all the godly taste from experience of divine protection. God’s power is infinite and invincible against the forces of the whole world. Measure God’s help not by human scale; despise terrors that stand in the way.

Reformed accent: shared—fearlessness before thousands. Courage fails unless this honor is ascribed to God; human arrays are little against him.

verses.text: Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! For you strike all my enemies on the cheek; you break the teeth of the wicked.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Cheek bone—contempt and reproach. Teeth—their strength and the instruments of their cruelty; he compares them to wild beasts.

Arminian hearing: shared plea—Arise, save! The God who sustains also strikes the wicked’s power. Prayer for salvation is not cancelled by prior sleep; keep asking while enemies still bite.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: after confidence he returns to prayer—save me, for peril remains. Smiting the cheek and breaking teeth he takes as thanksgiving for help already given, recognizing God as author of deliverance.

Reformed accent: shared—petition and praise. God shames and disarms the wicked; the servant both pleads and thanks for strikes already dealt.

verses.text: Salvation belongs to the LORD; your blessing be on your people! Selah
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley closes with the confession: salvation belongeth unto the LORD; thy blessing is upon thy people.

Arminian reading: shared doxology—salvation is God’s, not the crowd’s verdict. Those who cried and slept under his hand confess where help truly lies. Blessing on the people widens David’s rescue into care for the flock; hearers still look to the LORD alone for salvation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: salvation or deliverance is only in God’s hands—praise claimed for him alone against all human succor. A thousand deaths cannot render him unable to save. This was for the whole Church, whose welfare hung on the king’s safety; God will never withdraw grace and blessing from her.

Reformed accent: shared—salvation belongs to the LORD. The Church’s deliverance is secured by the God who saves without effort and keeps his blessing on his people.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess that salvation belongs to the LORD and that his blessing rests on his people—not on the many who denied help in God. Arminian readers stress the confessed dependence of those who cried, slept, and asked to be saved: deliverance is of the Lord and must be sought from him alone. Reformed readers, with Calvin, stress that saving power is God’s alone and that he will not withdraw grace and blessing from his Church—deliverance sure because it rests in his hands, not finally in the servant’s hold.
